units.t: How Many Friends Can You Really Have?.
Part one. The number one fifty.
Think about everyone you know well enough that, if you bumped into them at an airport at two in the morning, you wouldn't feel awkward joining them for a coffee.
Not your closest friends.
Not strangers. Just people you have a real, personal connection with.
How many would that be?
Twenty? A hundred?
A thousand?
In the early 1990s, a British researcher named Robin Dunbar came up with a surprisingly precise answer.
Dunbar is an anthropologist and evolutionary psychologist, and he spent much of his career at the University of Oxford.
He wasn't studying people at first.
He was studying monkeys and apes.
Dunbar noticed something about primates.
Species that live in bigger social groups tend to have a bigger neocortex, the wrinkly outer layer of the brain that handles complex thinking.
That made sense to him.
Keeping track of lots of relationships is hard mental work.
You need to remember who's friends with whom, who owes whom a favour, and who fell out with whom last week.
So Dunbar asked a simple question.
If we know the size of the human neocortex, what group size would the pattern predict for us?
The answer came out at roughly one hundred and fifty.
That figure is now known as Dunbar's number.
Here's the key point.
Dunbar wasn't saying you can only know one hundred and fifty names.
You probably recognise thousands of faces.
He was talking about meaningful relationships.
People you know as individuals, where you understand how they fit into your life and how they relate to each other.
Then he went looking for that number in the real world, and he kept finding something close to it.
Estimates for the size of early farming villages came out around there.
So did Hutterite communities, the religious farming groups in North America, which traditionally split into two once they grow much beyond that size.
Military companies across many armies tend to sit somewhere between about one hundred and two hundred people.
One of the most charming tests involved Christmas cards.
In a study with Russell Hill, Dunbar looked at who British households sent Christmas cards to.
The total number of people in those card networks averaged out at about one hundred and fifty.
So is one fifty a hard limit?
Not quite. And the more interesting story is what happens inside that number, which is where we're heading next.
Part two. Circles within circles.
Picture your social world as a set of rings, like the ripples when you drop a stone into a pond.
According to Dunbar's research, those rings have fairly predictable sizes.
Right at the centre, there are about five people.
These are the ones you'd call at three in the morning if something went badly wrong.
Partners, family members, your very closest friends.
Dunbar calls this the support clique.
The next ring holds about fifteen people in total, including those first five.
These are good friends.
People whose death would genuinely devastate you.
Then comes a ring of about fifty.
Think of them as the friends you'd invite to a big party or a barbecue.
After that comes the famous one hundred and fifty, the people you'd invite to a wedding or a big milestone birthday.
Notice the pattern.
Each ring is roughly three times the size of the one inside it.
Five, fifteen, fifty, one fifty.
The pattern even seems to continue outward, to about five hundred acquaintances and about fifteen hundred faces you can put a name to.
Why would our social lives be built like this?
A big part of the answer is time.
Friendship is expensive.
In one study, Dunbar and his colleagues found that people spend about forty per cent of their social time on those five closest people.
Another twenty per cent or so goes to the next ten.
That leaves surprisingly little for everyone else.
And friendships need that time to survive.
Dunbar's work suggests that if you stop seeing a friend, the emotional closeness starts to fade within months.
Family ties are more forgiving.
A cousin you rarely see is still a cousin.
Friendships, on the other hand, run on contact.
This also explains something many people notice in their own lives.
When someone starts a new romantic relationship, they often drift from a friend or two.
The new partner takes up one of those precious inner-circle places, and something else has to give.
One of Dunbar's studies suggested the typical cost was about two close friends.
So far this all sounds tidy.
But science rarely stays tidy for long, and Dunbar's number has had its critics.
That's where we'll finish.
Part three. What it means for you.
In 2021, a team at Stockholm University, led by Patrik Lindenfors, took another look at the primate brain data using newer statistical methods.
Their conclusion was blunt.
Depending on how you analyse the data, the predicted human group size could be almost anything, from a handful of people to several hundred.
In their view, you simply can't pin it to one hundred and fifty.
Dunbar and his supporters pushed back, pointing to the many real-world groups that cluster around that size.
The debate is still going.
So here's a fair way to hold it.
The exact number is contested.
The broader idea, that our close relationships are limited and come in layers, is widely accepted.
So what can you actually do with this?
Here are three practical ideas.
First, protect your inner five.
They get the largest share of your social time, and for good reason.
They're the people who carry you through hard times.
If one of those relationships has gone quiet lately, a phone call on your next drive might be the best use of ten minutes you'll have all week.
Second, remember that friendship takes time to build, not just to keep.
A researcher called Jeffrey Hall, at the University of Kansas, estimated how long it takes to turn an acquaintance into a friend.
His figures were roughly fifty hours together to become casual friends, around ninety hours to become real friends, and more than two hundred hours to become close friends.
That's why friendships formed at school, university or a new job feel so strong.
You were simply spending hours together without trying.
Third, don't feel guilty about the outer rings.
Nobody can be close to everyone.
Having a wider circle of friendly acquaintances is healthy and useful, and it's perfectly normal that you don't keep up with all of them.
Let's recap. Robin Dunbar suggested that humans can maintain around one hundred and fifty meaningful relationships.
Inside that number are layers of roughly five, fifteen and fifty, each about three times the size of the last.
The exact figure is debated, but the lesson holds.
Your time is limited, and where you spend it decides who stays close.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Roughly how many meaningful relationships does Dunbar's number suggest we can maintain?
Answer. About one hundred and fifty.
Question two. About how many people sit in the innermost support circle?
Answer. Around five.
Question three. According to Jeffrey Hall, roughly how many hours together does it take to become close friends?
Answer. More than two hundred hours.
That's the end of How Many Friends Can You Really Have? Nicely done.
